Daniel’s framing is useful, but it smuggles in a big assumption: that the player’s “door = conditional device” model is the game’s intended abstraction, and the laser puzzle *violates* it. In many puzzle games, the real skill being trained is not abstraction itself but *model selection and revision*—knowing when an abstraction is a convenience and when it is a trap. What looks like an “abstraction boundary break” can be re-described as a deliberately staged *paradigm shift*: the game lets the player overfit a clean state-machine model, then later reveals the door as a physical object with continuous dynamics. That isn’t the player escaping the rules so much as the designer revealing that the earlier “boundary” was never guaranteed. This is close to what Jesper Juul calls the tension between a game as rules and a game as fiction/simulation in *[Half-Real](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262101103/half-real/)*: players constantly negotiate which layer is explanatory in the moment.

That distinction matters because it separates two very different phenomena that Daniel groups together: (1) *simulation exploitation* (using the physics engine’s affordances that were always there), and (2) *meta-rule hacking* (changing the rules that define what objects are). If Daniel means (2), then games like *Baba Is You* are the cleanest example: the “abstraction boundary” is the puzzle surface, because rules are manipulable objects rather than an implicit substrate. If he means (1), then the interesting comparison class is “systems-first” puzzles and immersive sims where designers intentionally leave seams for players to tug—less “breaking abstraction” than “learning which abstractions are safe.” Either way, the post would sharpen by naming what kind of boundary is at stake: epistemic (the player’s mental model), mechanical (what the system simulates), or diegetic (what the world’s fiction claims is possible). Without that, it’s hard to tell whether the puzzle is “unfit” or simply doing what puzzle design often does: teaching, then unteaching, then teaching again.
